chapter_title: The Day the River Spoke (Learning Together)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Meeting Jahnavi: Pre-reading and First Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.1): close-eyes listening activity — oral sharing of sounds.
Let us read (p.1): predict Jahnavi's dream — paired oral sharing.

time_bands.activity: Open with the close-eyes listening prompt from 'Let us read' (p.1): ask students to sit quietly, notice every sound in the room, then share what they heard with a partner. Draw out the idea that sounds around us might be communicating something — a brief whole-class exchange to warm up their imagination.

Move to the second pre-reading prompt from 'Let us read' (p.1): tell students that Jahnavi is a bright girl in a coastal village with a dream, and ask pairs to predict what that dream could be and how she might pursue it. Take three or four responses before moving on.

Read aloud the prose text from p.1 to p.7 (Section I and early Section II) at an unhurried pace, pausing briefly after Jahnavi reaches the river and the River's voice is first heard — invite students to follow in their books and picture the kingfisher, the lizard, and the murmuring water.
Close by asking students to say one word that describes how Jahnavi is feeling by the river — take a quick round of answers to settle the reading in their minds before the unit ends.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading prompts are designed to lower the threshold for students who rarely speak — accept single-word answers and build on them without correction. The first reading of a personified River can confuse students who expect naturalistic narrative; pause just before the River's voice to ask 'Who do you think is speaking?' so the personification registers before the text names it. Task III (after Section I) is left unanchored here and can be used as a self-study prompt for students who finish reading early.

periods.activity_title: Jahnavi and the River: Comprehension and Extract Work

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.6): complete table matching Jahnavi's questions with River's answers.
Let us think and reflect (p.7): tone, phrase, punctuation, and qualities — Extract 1.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.7–8): Extract 2 questions on 'Can I do something?' — self-study.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the remaining prose from p.7 to p.8 (the section where the River encourages Jahnavi to go to school and Jahnavi finally does so) so the full story is in students' ears before comprehension work begins.

Work through 'Let us discuss' (p.6): display the two-column table on the board and invite students to call out Jahnavi's questions while you complete Column 1 together, then discuss the River's answers for Column 2 as a class, drawing on p.4–6 of the text.

Move to Extract 1 in 'Let us think and reflect' (p.7): read the extract aloud once, then work through all four sub-questions — tone identification, the phrase showing frequent visits, the punctuation effect of the exclamation mark, and the three qualities of the River — as a guided whole-class discussion with students marking answers in their books.
Summarise the River's character in one sentence together as a class — this consolidates the extract analysis before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read Jahnavi's journey to school, students are now ready to move from narrative to close analysis. The most common pitfall here is students treating the extract questions as opinion prompts — guide them back to the specific words of the extract each time. Extract 2 ('Can I do something?') is assigned for self-study at home; it follows the same pattern as Extract 1 and students can attempt it independently using p.7–8.
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for the two-column table

periods.activity_title: Deeper Reflection and Voices on Schooling

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — II (p.8): three reflective questions on nature, River's knowledge, and Jahnavi's age line.
Let us listen (p.39): circle words used by five speakers — first listening pass.
Let us listen (p.12): match seven statements to speakers — second listening pass.

time_bands.activity: Work through three questions from 'Let us think and reflect — II' (p.8): why nature is described in detail at the opening, how the River knew Jahnavi, and what Jahnavi's line 'I'm so old now' reveals about access to school — treat these as a discussion where students defend their readings with evidence from the prose.

Introduce the 'Let us listen' activity (p.39): read the ten words in the box aloud, then read the five speakers' transcripts clearly, one by one — ask students to circle the words they hear as you read.

Read the transcripts a second time for the matching task (p.12): students listen for which statement matches which speaker, filling in the table as they go — go over the answers as a class immediately after.
Briefly ask students: which speaker's view on schooling is closest to what the River told Jahnavi? One or two quick responses close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The critical-reading questions about nature description and the River's omniscience often produce shallow answers; prompt students to quote specific details from the opening paragraphs (kingfisher, lizard, rustling bamboo) to anchor their reasoning. For the listening task, reading the transcript slowly and clearly is essential — students who struggle with the matching exercise should be told the unused statements are 2 and 5, so they can check their reasoning rather than leaving blanks. Tasks 4 and 5 from 'Let us think and reflect — II' (on the River's laughter and Jahnavi's reasons to follow advice) are left unanchored for students to explore independently using p.8.

periods.activity_title: Finding Your Voice: Advice-Giving in Pairs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.13): deliver the River's sentence in different voices — paired turns.
Let us speak (p.13): ask for and give advice across four situations — paired role-play.

time_bands.activity: Read the River's sentence aloud ('Dear, dear! What's the matter? …') in a sleepy voice as a model, then ask students to identify what makes it sound sleepy — pace, pitch, pauses. This tunes their ears before they attempt their own versions.

Task I from 'Let us speak' (p.13): in pairs, students take turns delivering the same sentence in happy, surprised, angry, scared, sad, and worried voices — circulate and prompt students who stay flat by demonstrating one or two voices yourself.

Task II from 'Let us speak' (p.13): assign each pair one of the four situations (football team, maths nerves, music practice, blackboard visibility) and give them a quick paired exchange to rehearse; then rotate roles and try a second situation — invite two or three pairs to perform for the class, emphasising the advice-giving phrases on p.13.
Ask the class: what made the advice feel helpful rather than just a command? Take two quick answers to draw out the idea of tone and empathy in spoken language.

periods.teacher_notes: The story of Jahnavi asking the River for courage provides a direct model for the advice-giving register students are practising here — when students struggle to begin, remind them of the River's gentle, assuring tone with Jahnavi. A common pitfall in paired speaking is one student dominating; prompt the quieter partner by name and ensure role rotation happens. Students who finish the four situations can invent a fifth situation of their own, drawing on school life.

periods.activity_title: Observing Nature: From Notes to Descriptive Paragraph

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.14): plan and draft a descriptive nature paragraph using the prompts table.

time_bands.activity: Open the writing unit by asking students to look out of the window or recall a natural scene they know well — sky, a tree in the school yard, a nearby stream — and call out two textures, two colours, and one movement they notice or remember. Record five or six responses on the board as a shared bank of observations.

Model how the Ideas and Prompts table (p.14) structures a paragraph: walk through the six sentence starters ('Every day, I see…', 'I find it very interesting that…', etc.) on the board, drafting two sample sentences together as a class so students see how observation becomes prose.

Students write their own descriptive paragraph independently, using the prompts as scaffolding — circulate, reading over shoulders and nudging students to move from listing to describing (not just 'I see a tree' but 'I see a tree whose bark is rough and grey like cracked mud').

Peer response: students swap paragraphs with a neighbour, underline one strong image, and suggest one place where more detail would help — brief oral feedback, then students make one quick revision before the unit closes.
Ask one or two volunteers to read their opening sentence aloud — celebrate the variety of natural scenes chosen and close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Jahnavi's own curiosity about the natural world — the yellow spider in yellow flowers, the rustling bamboo, the moon's path — is a rich source of inspiration students can draw on for their paragraphs; pointing to these details from the story often unblocks students who feel they have nothing to say. The most common weakness in descriptive writing at this stage is a list without a feeling — the prompts 'I feel… as…' and 'I want to tell you that…' are particularly useful for pushing beyond inventory. The full draft, peer note, and one revision all happen within this unit so that no unfinished work is carried forward.

periods.activity_title: Sound Words, Prepositions, and the Capitalised River

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.8): why 'River' takes a capital letter — personification and nouns.
Let us learn (p.8–9): match sound words to definitions, then fill classroom-scene blanks.
Let us learn (p.11): fill blanks with correct prepositions — Jahnavi's first school day.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.11–12): fill blanks distinguishing prepositions from adverbs — self-study.

time_bands.activity: Begin with Task I (p.8): ask students why 'River' is capitalised in the story when it is a common noun — draw out the concept of personification through discussion, linking it to the River speaking, laughing, and showing care for Jahnavi.

Task II (p.8–9): display the nine definitions on the board; students work individually to match sound words from the text to the correct definition, then compare with a neighbour — go over answers as a class, reading each sound word aloud so students hear the word's texture (shriek, murmur, rustle, etc.). Then tackle the fill-in-the-blank classroom scene sentences together.

Task VI (p.11): read the six-sentence Jahnavi-at-school passage together, then students select the correct preposition from the brackets for each blank — go through answers sentence by sentence, asking students to explain why their choice fits (direction, location, or time).
Close with a quick question: can students find one more sound word in the prose that was not in the list? A two-minute hunt and one shared answer wraps the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The capitalisation of 'River' is the conceptual anchor for this entire vocabulary unit — personification as a literary device and as a grammatical choice are the same move, and linking them explicitly helps students see language as deliberate craft. Students often confuse 'murmur' (continuous background sound) with 'rustle' (dry, papery movement); play with the sounds of the words themselves to fix the distinction. Task VII (prepositions vs adverbs) and the loanword research task (Task III) are rich extensions; Task VII is set for home self-study, and Task III can be explored independently by students who enjoy language history.

periods.activity_title: Rivers, Languages, and the Girl-Child: Exploring Beyond the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.14): discuss why Indian rivers are considered sacred and gendered — whole-class.
Let us explore (p.15): read the poster 'Happiness of a Nation' and answer questions on dignity and happiness.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.15): find government schemes for girl-child education and plan neighbourhood awareness.

time_bands.activity: Open with Task I (p.14): ask students what they know about rivers being treated as sacred in India, then widen to the question of gendered names — why are most rivers referred to as female, and a few (Brahmaputra, Sone) as male? Accept geographical, cultural, and mythological reasons without privileging one; chart key ideas on the board.

Read the poster text 'The Happiness of a Nation lies in the Dignity of its Daughters' aloud (p.15), then work through the four questions from Task III: what is visible in the poster, why the girls look happy, the relationship between dignity and happiness, and how a nation prospers when its daughters are happy — alternate between pair discussion and whole-class sharing, asking students to build on each other's answers.

Briefly introduce Task IV (p.15) as a home inquiry project: students will find at least one government scheme for girl-child education and think about one way to share that information in their neighbourhood.

Close the unit by returning to the river: ask students — given everything they have discussed today, why do you think the author chose a river (and not a person) to counsel Jahnavi? Take two or three responses to bring the thematic exploration full circle.

periods.teacher_notes: The discussion on rivers and gender can touch on students' own regional traditions, which enriches the conversation considerably — encourage students from different language backgrounds to share what they know about river names in their home language. The poster analysis (Task III) works best when students treat 'dignity' as a concept to unpack from the ground up rather than a definition to memorise; the final question about national prosperity invites them to reason at a societal scale, which is appropriate for Grade VII. The whole-class language-mapping activity (Task II) is listed for home inquiry this unit; if class time allows, students can share results in a future free period.
materials: Chart paper and markers (optional, for river-name brainstorm)

items.source_lo: Student interprets character motivation and narrative craft using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Jahnavi's dream of schooling, the River's counsel, personification, and gender equality themes.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about Jahnavi and choose the option that correctly describes her reason for crying by the river. 
1. She was frightened that she was too old to begin school. 
2. She resented her brother Gopi for attending school instead of minding Appu. 
3. She had been kept home to care for younger siblings while other children went to school. 
4. She believed the teacher would never accept a girl into the classroom.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student has imported a detail not in the text — Jahnavi shows no resentment toward Gopi.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates over-reading: while statements 1 and 3 are supported, statement 2 is not evidenced in the prose.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misses statement 1 — Jahnavi explicitly fears she is too old, which is central to her hesitation.

items.source_lo: Student interprets character motivation and narrative craft using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Jahnavi's dream of schooling, the River's counsel, personification, and gender equality themes.
items.item_stem: In the story, the River is described as speaking in a sleepy, murmuring voice, yet it knows Jahnavi's name, her daily habits, and her hidden sorrow. The author also gives the River qualities such as gentle wit, assurance, and care. What does the author achieve by choosing a river — rather than a human character — to counsel Jahnavi, and how does this choice reinforce the story's theme of gender equality? Support your answer with two details from the prose.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: By personifying the River, the author presents a wise, impartial counsellor who stands outside human prejudice and social convention — unlike a person, the River cannot be accused of favouritism or defied on social grounds, which makes its message that 'little girls can do as much as little boys' more universally authoritative. This choice reinforces gender equality by showing that even nature itself affirms Jahnavi's right to schooling.

items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and matches speaker perspectives using a multi-voice listening text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five speakers on school life: freedom of choice, gendered access to schooling, vocational learning, companionship, and equal participation.
items.item_stem:
You will listen to five speakers talk about school life. Three of the following statements are true based on what the speakers say. Identify whether each statement is true or false.
1. The father believes that whether his child works in an organisation or stays at home should be the child's own choice.
2. The grandmother says she herself was never allowed to attend school.
3. The teacher mentions that school develops respect for head, hands, and heart.
4. The student says books help her learn about the world beyond her immediate surroundings.
5. The principal believes boys and girls should participate in different sets of activities.

options.text: The father believes that whether his child works in an organisation or stays at home should be the child's own choice.
The grandmother says she herself was never allowed to attend school.
The principal believes boys and girls should participate in different sets of activities.
The student says books help her learn about the world beyond her immediate surroundings.
The teacher mentions that school develops respect for head, hands, and heart.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — The father states education gives freedom of choice, whether his daughter works in an organisation or is a homemaker.
2. False — The grandmother says she went to school herself, though many girls around her could not.
3. True — The teacher explicitly names head, hands, and heart as values school develops.
4. True — The student says reading books helps her learn about things from all over the world.
5. False — The principal says students should take part in every activity, whether it is for girls or boys.

items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and matches speaker perspectives using a multi-voice listening text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five speakers on school life: freedom of choice, gendered access to schooling, vocational learning, companionship, and equal participation.
items.item_stem: After listening to all five speakers — the father, the grandmother, the teacher, the student, and the principal — which two speakers' views together come closest to the River's message to Jahnavi that girls have the same right to learn as boys? Write their roles (for example, 'father' or 'teacher') and give one reason for each choice, drawing on what each speaker said.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The father and the principal together come closest to the River's message. The father explicitly states that education should give his daughter freedom of choice equal to his son's — mirroring the River's point that girls can do as much as boys. The principal insists that every student should participate in every activity regardless of gender, reinforcing the same principle of equal access.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Jahnavi on the morning after she first attended school. You run back to the river to share your news. Speak two or three sentences aloud to the River, describing what you saw and felt in the classroom. Use a tone that is excited and relieved — the way someone feels when a fear has been overcome.

expected_elements: Uses first-person voice as Jahnavi, not a summary.
Tone is clearly excited or relieved — not flat or anxious.
Mentions at least one specific detail from the classroom scene.
Sentences are fluent and audible without reading from notes.

items.source_lo: Student uses spoken language to convey tone, ask for advice, and respond to real-life situations using guided conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Paired role-play: voice modulation on the River's sentence; advice-giving across school-life situations including gender barriers and academic anxiety.
items.item_stem: Work in a pair. One of you plays a student who wants to join the school's science club but has been told it is 'only for the top students.' The other plays an older friend giving advice, using the same kind of gentle, encouraging tone the River used with Jahnavi. Perform your conversation for the class — it should include the problem, at least one reason why the student has every right to try, and a clear piece of advice on what to do next.

expected_elements: Advice-giver uses an encouraging, non-dismissive tone throughout.
At least one reason given why the student has the right to try.
A concrete next step or action is suggested, not just reassurance.
Both speakers participate; dialogue is not a monologue.

items.item_stem: At the opening of the story, the author describes the river bank with specific details: a kingfisher swooping, a lizard basking in the sun, and the murmur of flowing water. Using these three elements as a starting point, write a short descriptive passage (four to five sentences) about the same scene. Include at least one colour, one texture, and one movement in your description. Give your passage a title.

expected_elements: A title is given that suits the scene described.
At least one colour, one texture, and one movement are named.
Sentences are descriptive, not merely listing objects.
Register is appropriate — vivid, sensory, neither too plain nor over-elaborate.

items.source_context: Descriptive paragraph on a natural scene — colours, textures, movement, light — using a structured prompt table.
items.item_stem: Jahnavi is curious about everything in nature — she wonders why spiders are yellow in yellow flowers, why bamboo rustles, and why the moon follows the same path. Imagine you are Jahnavi writing a personal journal entry the evening after the River first spoke to her. Describe one natural thing you have noticed that day, why it puzzles or delights you, and what you feel it is trying to tell you. Write a paragraph of at least six sentences. You may write from your own observations or imagine through Jahnavi's eyes.

expected_elements: Written as a journal entry — first person, personal and reflective tone.
One specific natural detail is named and described with curiosity.
A sense of wonder or emotional response is expressed, not just observation.
At least six sentences; language is imaginative, not purely factual.

items.item_stem: Match each sound word from the story with the action it describes. The words and their descriptions are given below.
items.visual_stimulus:
Sound word|Action it describes
murmur|a low, continuous, soft background sound
rustle|a soft, dry sound made by leaves or paper moving
gasp|a short, sharp intake of breath caused by surprise or shock
wail|a long, high-pitched cry of pain or sadness
shriek|a sudden, high-pitched piercing sound

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: murmur – a low, continuous, soft background sound; rustle – a soft, dry sound made by leaves or paper moving; gasp – a short, sharp intake of breath caused by surprise or shock; wail – a long, high-pitched cry of pain or sadness; shriek – a sudden, high-pitched piercing sound.

answer_key.right: a low, continuous, soft background sound
a soft, dry sound made by leaves or paper moving
a short, sharp intake of breath caused by surprise or shock
a long, high-pitched cry of pain or sadness

items.item_stem: In the story, the author writes 'River' with a capital letter even though it is a common noun. A student reading the story said: 'The author must have made a spelling mistake.' Write two or three sentences explaining whether the student is correct, and what the capitalisation actually tells a careful reader about the way the River is presented in the story.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The student is incorrect — the capitalisation is a deliberate literary choice, not an error. The author capitalises 'River' because it is personified throughout the story: it speaks, laughs, shows care, and gives advice, behaving as a named character rather than a natural feature. Capitalising it signals to the reader that this River has a personality and a voice, just as a proper name signals a distinct individual.

items.item_stem: The poster in your textbook reads: 'The Happiness of a Nation lies in the Dignity of its Daughters.' The word 'dignity' means self-respect. Write a paragraph of four to six sentences explaining how this idea connects to what happens to Jahnavi in the story — and what one thing a school, family, or community could do to put this idea into practice.

expected_elements: Connects 'dignity' to Jahnavi's specific experience — being denied school or gaining access.
Identifies at least one way the story shows respect for a girl's self-worth.
Names one concrete action a school, family, or community could take.
Paragraph is coherent and stays on the theme of dignity and education.

items.item_stem: In the story, Jahnavi's mother says that she herself once longed for school but was denied by her own mother. The story spans at least two generations of girls being kept from education. Design a short awareness project (you may describe it in writing or as a plan) that a student your age could carry out in their neighbourhood to inform families about one government scheme supporting the education of girls. Your plan should state: (a) the name of any one government scheme you know, (b) the audience you are targeting, and (c) two specific actions you would take to spread awareness.

expected_elements: Names at least one real government scheme for girl-child education.
Identifies a specific audience — families, younger children, the locality.
Proposes two distinct, feasible awareness actions (poster, skit, home visit, etc.).
Connects the project to the story's theme of access to education.
